Hypocritical
hĭp-ō-krĭt´ĭ-kăl
adj. (playing a part; profane under a religious appearance — rendering Hebrew chaneph)
Greek hupokrites, a stage-player, one who answers from under a mask. The Hebrew chaneph is stronger and darker: soiled with sin, profane, godless under a cover.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hypocritical in the Old Testament translates a Hebrew word that means profane or polluted — not merely inconsistent but godless beneath a covering. David describes his tormentors: “With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth” (Psa 35:16). Isaiah applies the word to a whole people under judgment: “I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey” (Isa 10:6). That is the terrible use. A nation may keep its temple, its sacrifices and its feasts, and be called hypocritical by God because the religion covers a heart at war with Him. The Lord Jesus names the same condition in its most respectable form: “Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Mat 23:28). And Bildad, for all his hardness toward Job, states the settled truth: “So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish” (Job 8:13). The hypocrite is not a man who fails to live up to his profession — that describes every Christian — but a man whose profession is the covering rather than the confession of what he is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hypocritical as counterfeiting a good character; dissembling; insincere; applied to one who assumes an appearance of piety and virtue when he is destitute of them.

expand to see more

HYPOCRIT'ICAL, a. Counterfeiting a good character which one has not; dissembling; insincere.

2. Proceeding from hypocrisy, or marking hypocrisy; as, hypocritical professions.

HYP'OCRITE, n. One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power, or who assumes an appearance of piety and virtue when he is destitute of true religion.

HYPOC'RISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; particularly, the assuming of a false appearance of virtue or religion.

Key Scripture

Psalm 35:16 — "With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth."

Isaiah 10:6 — "I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets."

Matthew 23:28 — "Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity."

Job 8:13 — "So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish:"

Modern Corruption

The charge of hypocrisy is turned against anyone who holds a standard he has not perfectly kept, so that the word now condemns conviction instead of pretence.

expand to see more

The commonest use of the word today is an accusation aimed at any Christian who names a sin he has himself committed, or who upholds a standard he has failed. That is not what Scripture means. A man who confesses a standard, breaks it, and repents is not a hypocrite; he is a sinner behaving as a believer ought. The hypocrite of Matthew 23 is the man who outwardly appears righteous unto men while inwardly full of iniquity — whose religion is the mask, not the confession. Redefining the word as it is now used has a convenient effect: it silences moral speech altogether, since no one may name a sin he has not perfectly overcome.

The second thing the word exposes is corporate. Isaiah 10:6 calls an entire covenant nation hypocritical, with its worship still running, and sends a pagan empire against it. That judgment falls on a people whose religion had become a covering over injustice, and the prophets are explicit about what was under the covering — the fatherless not judged, the widow's cause not heard, hands full of blood. A church or a nation may keep every ordinance and be under this word. The remedy is never to abandon the forms but to be what the forms declare, and to begin the reckoning at the house of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chaneph (H2611), profane, polluted, godless — rendered hypocritical in Psalm 35:16 and Isaiah 10:6; Greek hupokrisis (G5272) and hupokrites (G5273), the stage-player.

expand to see more

Hebrew chaneph (H2611) — soiled with sin, profane; Job 8:13, Psalm 35:16, Isaiah 10:6.

Hebrew chanaph (H2610) — to be polluted, defiled; used of a land defiled by bloodshed, Numbers 35:33.

Greek hupokrites (G5273) — an actor under an assumed character; the Lord's word for the scribes and Pharisees.

Greek hupokrisis (G5272) — the playing of the part; Matthew 23:28, Galatians 2:13, 1 Timothy 4:2.

The Hebrew is heavier than the Greek: not merely feigning, but profane beneath the appearance.

Usage

"“An hypocritical nation” — the temple still running, the heart at war."

"“Outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within…” — the mask defined."

"“The hypocrite's hope shall perish” — the one hope that has nothing under it."
